entries.why_wrong: sort() does mutate the array in place, but that's not what breaks this function — the returned array still contains all four scores. The real problem is the ordering itself: without a comparator, `[10, 9, 2, 21]` gets compared as strings, so `10` sorts before `2`.

Switching to a for loop would just mean writing your own sort algorithm from scratch — sort() itself can absolutely handle numeric arrays correctly. It just needs an explicit comparator like `(a, b) => a - b` instead of relying on the default lexicographic string comparison.

sort() never throws on numbers; it happily accepts any array and just calls a default comparison that treats every element as a string. That silent string coercion, not a crash, is why `[10, 9, 2, 21]` comes out as `[10, 2, 21, 9]`.
